latin.meaning: lasting through the year; everlasting, perpetual, unceasing
latin.forms: perennis, perenne (nom. sg. masc./fem., neut.); declined as a third-declension adjective of two terminations
latin.etymology: From per- (through) + annus (year), literally 'lasting through the year,' extended to mean perpetual or eternal.
latin.literary_context: Horace uses perennis in his famous claim of poetic immortality: 'Exegi monumentum aere perennius' (I have built a monument more lasting than bronze) in Odes 3.30, asserting his verses will outlive physical monuments.
latin.usage_example: Non omnis moriar multaque pars mei vitabit Libitinam; usque ego postera crescam laude recens, dum Capitolium scandet cum tacita virgine pontifex. — I shall not wholly die, and a great part of me will escape the goddess of death; I shall grow ever fresh in the praise of posterity, as long as the pontiff climbs the Capitoline with the silent virgin.
latin.did_you_know: The English word 'perennial' derives directly from perennis, retaining both the botanical sense (plants living multiple years) and the figurative sense of something enduring or constantly recurring.

greek.forms: nom. ἀναγνώρισις, gen. ἀναγνωρίσεως, dat. ἀναγνωρίσει, acc. ἀναγνώρισιν; plural ἀναγνωρίσεις
greek.etymology: From ἀνα- (again, back) + γνωρίζω (to make known, recognize), from γνῶσις (knowledge). The verb γιγνώσκω (to know) comes from the Indo-European root *ǵneh₃-.
greek.literary_context: Aristotle in the Poetics defines ἀναγνώρισις as a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing friendship or enmity in those destined for good or bad fortune; he identifies the recognition between Oedipus and Jocasta as a prime example of tragic anagnorisis.
greek.usage_example: ἡ δὲ ἀναγνώρισις ἐστὶν ἐξ ἀγνοίας εἰς γνῶσιν μεταβολή. — Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge.
greek.did_you_know: Aristotle considered anagnorisis most effective when it coincides with peripeteia (reversal), as in Oedipus Rex, where Oedipus discovers his true identity at the moment his fortune collapses, making it the paradigmatic example of tragic structure.

french.etymology: From Latin philtrum, from Greek φίλτρον (phíltron) 'love charm,' derived from φιλεῖν (phileîn) 'to love.' The word entered French in the 12th century.
french.literary_context: Racine employs this word in Phèdre (1677), where the titular character attributes her forbidden passion for Hippolyte to Venus's vengeance, invoking the imagery of supernatural forces and enchantments that render her powerless.
french.usage_example: Elle croyait avoir bu quelque philtre empoisonné. — She believed she had drunk some poisoned potion.
french.did_you_know: The distinction between philtre (potion) and filtre (filter) was maintained in French spelling until 1935, when the Académie française accepted both spellings for the straining device, though philtre retained its specialized meaning of magical drink.

german.forms: das Schicksal; gen. des Schicksals; pl. die Schicksale
german.etymology: From Middle High German 'schicksal', derived from 'schicken' (to send, arrange) + '-sal' (noun suffix indicating result or state). The root connects to the notion of what is 'sent' or 'arranged' by higher powers.
german.literary_context: Schiller employs Schicksal throughout his dramas, most notably in 'Wallenstein' where the general's tragic downfall hinges on his belief in astrological fate. Hölderlin invokes it in 'Hyperion' as the force that both separates and binds the protagonist to his beloved Diotima.
german.usage_example: Der Mensch kann dem Schicksal nicht entfliehen, aber er kann ihm mit Würde begegnen. — Man cannot escape fate, but he can meet it with dignity.
german.did_you_know: Nietzsche transformed the concept of Schicksal through 'amor fati' (love of fate), arguing that affirmation of necessity rather than passive submission represents the highest human achievement. This reinterpretation inverts the traditional German Romantic view of fate as tragic inevitability.

oldenglish.forms: nom./acc. sg. bānhūs; gen. sg. bānhūses; dat. sg. bānhūse; nom./acc. pl. bānhūs
oldenglish.etymology: Compound of bān 'bone' (from Proto-Germanic *bainą) + hūs 'house' (from Proto-Germanic *hūsą). This kenning reflects the Anglo-Saxon poetic conception of the body as a dwelling for the soul.
oldenglish.literary_context: The word appears in the Old English poem The Seafarer, where the speaker reflects on mortality and the transience of earthly existence. Similar body-kennings pervade heroic verse, emphasizing the physical shell's vulnerability.
oldenglish.usage_example: Þonne bið gehwyrfed bānhūs blāte. — Then the body is turned pale.
oldenglish.did_you_know: Anglo-Saxon poets developed dozens of kennings for the human body, including feorhhūs (life-house), flæschoma (flesh-covering), and līchama (body-garment), each emphasizing different aspects of embodied existence and mortality.
